title: Ki-67 as an Intermediate Endpoint in Cancer Interception: Current Evidence and Future Directions
content: Background/Objectives: Cancer interception trials require intermediate endpoints capable of detecting biologic activity before cancer incidence, progression, or survival outcomes become measurable. Ki-67, a nuclear marker of cellular proliferation, is widely used as a prognostic and pharmacodynamic biomarker across multiple malignancies. This review evaluates the evidence supporting Ki-67 modulation as an intermediate endpoint in cancer interception and prevention research. Methods: Published clinical studies reporting pre- and post-intervention Ki-67 changes were reviewed, with emphasis on interception, prevention, and presurgical window-of-opportunity trials involving dietary, phytochemical, and endocrine interventions. Results: Evidence from prostate, lung, and breast cancer settings demonstrates that Ki-67 is responsive to biologic intervention. In CAPFISH-3, a high omega-3/low omega-6 dietary intervention plus fish oil reduced Ki-67 by 15% in men undergoing active surveillance for prostate cancer, whereas Ki-67 increased by 24% in controls. In a randomized phase II lung premalignancy trial, a sulforaphane-producing intervention reduced bronchial Ki-67 by 20%, compared with a 65% increase with placebo. Presurgical breast cancer studies, including flaxseed supplementation and endocrine therapy trials, further demonstrated significant reductions in Ki-67 over short intervention periods. However, changes in Ki-67 were not consistently accompanied by short-term histologic or clinical endpoint improvements. Conclusions: Current evidence supports Ki-67 as a promising intermediate pharmacodynamic endpoint capable of detecting biologic activity in cancer interception studies. Nevertheless, variability in assessment methods, tissue sampling, and uncertainty regarding long-term clinical correlation limit its current role as a surrogate endpoint. Additional prospective validation is required before Ki-67 can be adopted as a standardized endpoint in cancer interception research.
